name: William IV
role: King of the United Kingdom (1830–1837); earlier naval officer and Duke of Clarence
summary: A naval officer turned king whose recorded political stance is thin and mostly conservative. As Duke of Clarence he spoke in the Lords against limiting the slave trade, citing West India property, and later he accepted the Whigs and the Reform Act only reluctantly, resisting mass creation of peers. In 1834 he dismissed the Melbourne ministry, partly over fears of radicalism and Church reform.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: In his 1799 Lords speech he opposed limiting the slave trade, and in his first speech described enslaved people as in a state of humble happiness; he called abolitionists fanatics or hypocrites. Quote reported secondhand, speech arguments in his published text.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Reigned as king and asserted a personal role, saying he told ministers his view of things, and dismissed the Melbourne ministry in 1834 on his own initiative.

gradual-change.rationale: Accepted reform only reluctantly and tried to limit new peerages to eldest sons and heirs; in 1834 feared Whig reforms would go too far without Althorp's restraint. Mixed with his acceptance of the Reform Act, so low.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: His 1834 dismissal of the ministry was reported to rest partly on worry about ministers' plans to reform the English and Irish churches. Reported motive, not his own stated words.

property-fundamental.rationale: In 1799 he rested his argument on the roughly 100 million pounds of West India property tied to the slave trade and urged the Lords as guardians of subjects' property to protect it; argued for a specific trade, not a general principle.

military-superiority.rationale: As king he pressed naval readiness: gunnery, readiness reports and more steam warships.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Said a constitutional monarch cannot act against Parliament's opinion, yet dismissed a ministry that held a Commons majority and, earlier, refused Grey's request to swamp the Lords.

notes: Reform Act 1832, abolition of slavery 1833 and Poor Law 1834 are not counted as his positions (assent on ministers' advice). Direct Hansard pages and the Grey letters could not be fetched; Wikipedia's quoted remarks are secondhand.
